title: How Foreign Investors Can Set Up a Company in Nepal in 2025
content:
Foreign Direct Investment (FDI) has become one of the most discussed topics in Nepal's economic policy. As the government continues to liberalise the investment climate, foreign companies are exploring entry into sectors ranging from hydropower and tourism to manufacturing and information technology.

Legal framework for foreign investment

The principal legislation governing foreign investment is the Foreign Investment and Technology Transfer Act (FITTA), 2075, read together with the Companies Act, 2063. FITTA establishes the framework for foreign investment approval, repatriation rights, and sectoral limits, while the Companies Act governs how a foreign-owned entity is formed and administered.

Choosing the right corporate structure

Most foreign investors incorporate either a private limited company or a public limited company under the Companies Act, 2063. The private limited structure remains the most common for wholly owned subsidiaries because it offers flexibility in governance and simpler reporting obligations.

Step-by-step incorporation process

The typical process of establishing a company in Nepal involves the following steps:

  • Name clearance from the Office of the Company Registrar
  • Drafting and notarising the memorandum and articles of association
  • Filing incorporation documents and obtaining the certificate of incorporation
  • Registering with the tax authority and obtaining a Permanent Account Number (PAN)
  • Opening a corporate bank account and, where applicable, registering for VAT

Approvals and clearances

Depending on the sector and investment size, investors may require approval from the Investment Board Nepal (IBN), the Department of Industry, or the Nepal Rastra Bank for capital inflow and repatriation. Sector regulators such as the Nepal Electricity Authority or the Nepal Rastra Bank may impose additional licensing conditions.

Key considerations for 2025

Foreign investors should plan for rising compliance expectations around beneficial ownership disclosure, anti-money-laundering rules, and sector-specific licensing. Companies incorporated with a minimum foreign shareholding often face additional audit and reporting duties, so engaging local counsel early reduces delay significantly.

title: Key Corporate Law Reforms in Nepal: What Directors Need to Know
content:
Directors of companies in Nepal operate under a steadily evolving statutory regime. Recent amendments and regulatory practice have tightened director accountability, expanded disclosure duties, and reshaped how boards manage conflicts of interest. Staying current is no longer optional.

The Companies Act, 2063 as the cornerstone

The Companies Act, 2063 remains the primary source of directors' duties. It codifies fiduciary obligations to act in good faith, avoid conflicts of interest, and exercise the care and diligence of a reasonably prudent person in the same circumstances.

Board responsibilities that receive scrutiny

Regulators increasingly focus on the following areas:

  • Timely and accurate financial reporting to shareholders and the Office of the Company Registrar
  • Proper maintenance of statutory registers and minutes of board meetings
  • Disclosure of transactions with related parties and connected persons
  • Compliance with beneficial ownership reporting under anti-money-laundering rules
  • Approval of significant asset transfers and major financing arrangements

Conflicts of interest

A director who has an interest in a transaction must disclose it and, in most cases, abstain from the relevant board resolution. Failure to do so can expose the director to personal liability and void the transaction at the instance of the company.

Insolvency and personal liability

Recent judicial trends have made directors personally accountable for trading while the company is insolvent and for preferences that prejudice creditors. Boards facing distress should seek advice before continuing operations.

Practical steps for 2026

Directors should schedule annual governance reviews, update the company's internal bylaws, and verify that statutory filings are current. External counsel can help audit board practices against emerging expectations.

title: Trademark Registration in Nepal: A Practical Guide for Businesses
content:
Brands are among the most valuable assets a business owns, yet many companies in Nepal operate without registered trademark protection. Registration grants a statutory monopoly over the mark and provides a strong basis for enforcement against counterfeiters and copycats.

Where to file

Trademarks are registered with the Department of Industry under the Patent, Design and Trademark Act, 2022. The same office administers patents, industrial designs, and trademarks, so the system operates centrally in Kathmandu.

The registration process

The application process generally involves:

  • Conducting a preliminary search to identify conflicting marks
  • Filing the application with a representation of the mark and details of the applicant
  • Examination by the Department of Industry
  • Publication and, where no opposition succeeds, registration of the mark

Distinctiveness matters

The mark must be capable of distinguishing the applicant's goods or services. Descriptive words and common surnames are frequently rejected unless they have acquired secondary meaning through use.

Duration and renewal

A registered trademark is initially valid for a period of seven years and may be renewed for successive periods. Renewal is a relatively simple filing, but missing the deadline can result in the mark being removed from the register.

Enforcing your rights

Registered proprietors can oppose conflicting applications, demand cessation of infringing use, and pursue civil remedies or criminal action. Unregistered marks depend on passing off, which is more difficult and expensive to establish.

title: Renewable Energy Projects in Nepal: Legal and Regulatory Overview
content:
Nepal's renewable energy sector, led by hydropower, continues to attract domestic and foreign investment. Understanding the licensing, environmental, and power-purchase framework is essential before committing capital to a project.

Primary legislation

The Electricity Act, 2049 and the Electricity Regulations, 2050 govern the generation, transmission, and distribution of electricity. The Investment Board Act applies to larger projects that fall within the national priority thresholds.

Licensing requirements

Project developers must obtain:

  • A survey licence to conduct preliminary studies and feasibility assessments
  • An electricity generation licence once the survey and studies are complete
  • Approval of the environmental impact assessment (EIA) or initial environmental examination (IEE), as applicable

Power purchase agreements

The Nepal Electricity Authority (NEA) is the principal off-taker. The terms of the power purchase agreement (PPA), including tariffs and take-or-pay obligations, are negotiated against the prevailing regulatory framework and can significantly affect bankability.

Project finance considerations

Lenders typically require a complete chain of land rights, generation and transmission licences, a signed PPA, and adequate insurance. Foreign investors should also confirm whether the investment requires approval from the Investment Board Nepal or sectoral regulators.

Environmental and social compliance

Hydropower and renewable projects face heightened environmental and social scrutiny. Resettlement, forest clearance, and river-flow obligations must be addressed in the EIA and monitored through the project lifecycle.

title: Employment Law in Nepal: Employee Rights and Employer Obligations
content:
The Labor Act, 2074 is the central statute governing employment relationships in Nepal. It applies to most private sector employers and prescribes minimum standards for contracts, working hours, leave, termination, and social security.

Written employment contracts

Employers must provide a written contract or appointment letter to every employee. The document should set out the nature of work, remuneration, working hours, and the grounds and procedure for termination.

Working hours and leave

The standard working week is limited to 48 hours, with overtime payable for additional work. Employees are entitled to annual leave, sick leave, and public holidays, together with maternity and paternity leave as prescribed by the statute.

Termination and severance

Termination must follow the procedure in the Labor Act. Employees whose services are terminated, other than for misconduct, are entitled to notice or pay in lieu, together with gratuity and leave encashment where applicable.

Social security

Registered employers must contribute to the Social Security Fund on behalf of their employees. Contributions cover medical, accident, dependency, and pension benefits, and late or non-payment attracts penalties.

Practical compliance steps

Employers should maintain proper attendance records, payroll documentation, and statutory registers, and ensure that workplace policies comply with anti-discrimination and occupational safety obligations.
